author.name: James Joyce
author.biography: Joyce left Ireland as a young man, but Dublin remained at the centre of his imagination. Financial insecurity, family responsibilities and problems with his eyesight accompanied a literary career that repeatedly met resistance from publishers and censors. Joyce wrote much of his great Dublin novel while living abroad. Distance became an occasion to reconstruct the city's streets, voices and smallest daily habits.

hook.text: What if your ordinary day were an epic?

paragraphs: Leopold Bloom has errands to do. He will eat, walk through Dublin, attend a funeral and look for somewhere to spend the hours. Stephen Dedalus is moving through the same city with a different burden of memories. It is 16 June 1904. A very ordinary day is about to become an enormous book.

Joyce gives passing thoughts the attention usually reserved for heroic deeds. Hunger, embarrassment, desire, grief and stray advertising slogans share a person's mind. A city lives through the voices people overhear as much as through the events anyone thinks worth recording.

The writing keeps changing its rules. A chapter may imitate a newspaper, a catechism or a theatrical spectacle. Some of this will be puzzling. Much of it is funny, bodily and unexpectedly tender. You do not have to catch every reference to recognise the wish to be welcomed somewhere.

Homer supplies a distant pattern, but Bloom earns our attention through the ordinary work of getting through a day among other people. How much of a life becomes visible when we stop deciding in advance what deserves to count?

orientation.text: The eighteen episodes change style. Follow Bloom and Stephen through the day before trying to solve every allusion; unfamiliar passages can be revisited.
